title: Disney+ Signs Content Deal With Gary Neville’s The Overlap To Strike Back Against Netflix’s Football Podcast Play
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse ‘Son Of A Critch’: Trailer For Final Season Of Canadian Sitcom Sees Mark Having A Midlife Crisis At 17 Actor & Singer Luke Charles Stafford Launches Dream United Studios With ‘Against The Wall’ Magna Studios Signs ‘20,000 Days On Earth’ Makers Iain Forsyth & Jane Pollard View All August 13, 2026 2:48am Disney+ has signed a podcast deal with The Overlap Disney+ The score is now Disney+ 1, Netflix 1. Disney’s streaming service has struck a deal with former Manchester United footballer and emerging media magnate Gary Neville for podcasts from his Global Studios-owned company, The Overlap . This follows Netflix branching out into football podcasts over the summer by backing the World Cup editions of Gary Lineker’s show , The Rest is Football . The arrangement highlights the growing power of podcasts led by former players, and the desire for global streamers to sign up video-led sports podcasts. The agreement sees Disney+ land 40 new episodes of Neville’s Stick to Football show, with the streamer also getting 50 episodes of new series Stick to United with Wayne Rooney . Disney+ will become headline sponsor on both shows during the nearing 2026/27 season. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News 'The Lowdown' Gets Season 2 Release Date At FX; First Photos Of Tommy Lee Jones & Betty Gilpin News Alex Cooper's Unwell Media Company Valued At $500M After Investment By Patrick Whitesell's Firm The Stick to Football episodes will run on Disney+, other podcast platforms and The Overlap’s YouTube channel, while Stick to United will be on Disney+, other platforms and The Overlap. Twenty episodes will be exclusive to Disney+ for a “limited time.” Disney+ has also commissioned six exclusive extended-length eps of Stick to United that will feature special guests. Stick to Football is hosted by footballing legends Neville, Jamie Carragher, Jill Scott, Ian Wright and Roy Keane, and sees the group welcome guests to discuss all manner of football matters. Stick to United will see Manchester United record goalscorer Rooney, who was a breakout pundit at the recent World Cup, hosting alongside Mark Goldbridge , the often over-excited and exasperated United fan who has built a huge YouTube following for his views on the team’s performances. They will analyze the English Premier League team’s latest results and biggest talking points. Goldbridge sold his media channels to The Overlap in April, and today he called Stick to United “an historic milestone for fan-led media.” Stick to United will stream weekly from next Tuesday (August 18), while Stick to Football will stream weekly in the UK and Ireland from Thursday (August 20). Neville, co-founder and co-chair of The Overlap, said the “unique partnership that feels right for everyone involved,” and added, “What’s exciting is that we’re not changing who we are. Our community will continue to enjoy our content in exactly the way they always have through YouTube, while at the same time Disney+’s incredible global streaming audience will now be able to discover and enjoy it too.” “As we move into a new era of sports entertainment on Disney+, we’re excited to be bringing one of the UK’s most popular and distinctive sports shows to the platform,” said Sean Doyle, Disney+ EMEA’s VP, Unscripted. “What Gary and the team at The Overlap have created with Stick to Football – and now Stick to United with Wayne Rooney – is truly unique. Adding both shows broadens our local original content offering as we continue to expand into new sports formats, complementing our existing catalogue of drama, comedy, documentary, reality and ESPN on Disney+.” Global, the UK-based radio and audio giant, acquired a majority stake in The Overlap in January. Noah Schnapp , best known as Will Byers in “ Stranger Things ,” is set to make his world stage debut in the British capital. The actor, who became a household name thanks to the Netflix phenomenon, is adding theater to his resume as the star of “Affluenza” at Riverside Studios as part of its Mainstage Season 26/27. Related Stories Spain's World Cup Triumph Gets Prime Video Series 'The Traitors' India Season 2 Unveils Trailer With Karan Johar and 21-Celebrity Cast (EXCLUSIVE) Written and directed by Mainstage Season artistic director Andy Sandberg and running Sep. 26 to Nov. 21, “Affluenza” is set against the ultra-wealthy social haven of the Hamptons, and is described as raising “thought-provoking questions about moral accountability, family legacy, and the American justice system.” Popular on Variety In the play, when a teen’s drunken car ride ends in devastation, the verdict comes down to one question – is it possible to be too affluent to know the difference between right and wrong? Inspired by true events surrounding a shocking legal defence, “Affluenza” explores the “ripple effects of power and privilege.” “I am so excited to make my stage debut in London with ‘Affluenza,'” said Schnapp. “I started talking with Andy Sandberg a few months ago about finding the right opportunity to work together, and it’s thrilling to now be bringing this play to life in London. I wanted to be very intentional about what I took on next, and as I spend more time with this excellent script, I feel so connected to the characters. Without giving away too much, I get to play two very different roles, and it’s a story that’s really going to leave audiences talking and thinking.” “Affluenza” opens Riverside’s Mainstage Season 26/27, which comprises five new plays, largely set in contemporary America and exploring globally relevant themes. “I am incredibly excited to be launching this play and this season in just a few weeks — and now with Noah Schnapp at the helm,” said Sandberg, a Tony-winning producer who also serves as Mainstage Season artistic director. “Noah is a brilliant young actor who has captivated audiences on screen, and now London audiences will have the opportunity to see him in his stage debut. I’m honoured that Noah has connected with the script, and I think it speaks volumes that he has chosen an original play for his stage debut.” Following “Affluenza” the season will continue with “Sacrilegious,” by Tom Schulman, the Oscar-winning writer of “Dead Poets Society” and “Honey, I Shrunk the Kids,” and “Expecting,” by Scott Elmegreen and Drew Fornarola. Both are being are directed by Sandberg, who also serves as artistic director for the Hermitage in the U.S. Further productions and casting will be announced soon. title: Asia Argento Discusses Playing “a Racist,” Locarno Honor and Exec-Producing a Gia Carangi Doc
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 13, 2026 1:30am Asia Argento Courtesy of Fabrizio Cestari Italian actress, filmmaker and musician Asia Argento is about to take the big outdoor stage in Locarno in the Italian-speaking part of Switzerland. The 79 th edition of the Locarno Film Festival will celebrate the creative with its Life Achievement Award on Thursday evening in the city’s Piazza Grande in front of around 8,000 people. While in Locarno, Argento is also presenting Jorge Thielen Armand’s Death Has No Master ( La Muerte No Tiene Dueño ), which premiered in this year’s Cannes Directors’ Fortnight. “Since making her onscreen debut as a child in Lamberto Bava’s cult sequel Demons 2 (1986) and starring in Palombella rossa (1989) by Nanni Moretti, Asia Argento , one of the most distinctive European performers of her generation, has built a singular body of work that encompasses passionately beloved genre films, auteur cinema, and intimate self-portraiture,” Locarno said when it unveiled the honor. And Giona A. Nazzaro , Locarno’s artistic director, lauded her as “an artist who has always managed to reimagine what it means to make films, constantly challenging herself and taking personal risks.” Related Stories Movies Zurich Film Fest Galas Set for Award Contenders 'I Play Rocky,' 'Possible Love,' 'Josephine' News Analysis The Emmys Rules Are Excluding Tons of Great International TV Argento spoke to THR about the honor, her role in Death Has No Master and the documentary about late U.S. supermodel Gia Carangi that she has boarded as an executive producer. Congratulations on the special Locarno honor. How does it feel to get this recognition? It feels incredible. I truly didn’t expect it. Actually, lately I was thinking, my God, I’ve never been invited to Locarno, and I never had a movie at Locarno. I was self-deprecating as usual, thinking they must hate me and everyone is against me. And then this came totally out of the blue, and I was moved to tears. In the last few years, I had a big shift of energy, and I guess life has a way of teaching you to be humble sometimes when you don’t want to learn. So I see this as a sign of the universe that I’m going in the right direction. With my work, I was in the past [sometimes] criticized for it being a little bit extreme and pushing the boundaries of what was accepted from a woman, as an actress, as a filmmaker. What I was trying to achieve created this gut unease, and now this is a way of the universe telling me that I did the right thing at the right time. When you pass through a door, you always receive a lot of blows to your head, so that other people can walk through it a little bit more easily. Now I see that everything is making sense. Okay, I wasn’t wrong to always be who I was, to be honest about who I was, even though I’m somebody who’s far from being perfect. It was a big shine of love. You are presenting Jorge Thielen Armand’s postcolonial thriller Death Has No Master ( La Muerte No Tiene Dueño ), in which you star, at Locarno. Why did you want to work on that film with its themes of colonialism and trauma? What about it spoke to you? I always find characters that are nonlinear, that are a bit tormented and that have a vast history and things to face from the past fascinating. I like complex characters with a lot of suffering. I find it a lot easier and more interesting to do that than, say, a comedy, which I’ve done in my life, and I’m not very talented at that. It’s really not my genre. So when I find something really dark, really obscure and weird with depth, then I dive into that. I just read the script, and I also loved the idea of the adventure of going to Venezuela and this challenge of also acting in yet another language, Spanish, since I’ve done French and English. It was also a huge challenge physically and mentally. At this point in my life, I prefer the challenges that keep me curious and keep me alert. Asia Argento in ‘Death Has No Master.’ Cannes Film Festival How was the production of the film? It was very tough to shoot. I didn’t immediately understand from the script that it would turn into a psychological thriller, almost paranormal in a way. I thought it was a colonial drama about family history and all that, but it’s a lot more than that. And when I saw the movie, I was so immersed in the experience. Jorge is such a great director. I love his movies, and I think that with this one, he found yet another register to his art. So just working there with him fueled my fire and my love. Speaking about colonialism: How do you get into a role like this? Did you ever travel and experience the weight of colonialism? Or how do you find the access point as an actress to something that is so painful for so many people? It was pretty hard, because we developed the script and the character a lot while we rehearsed for a month before the shoot in the locations with all the non-actors there. As we were preparing, I realized, “My God, my character is a racist; she’s really not somebody that I would like to meet.” To play that, you have to really understand and love to prepare for that. I was in Venezuela. There were a lot of stories about the richer people that went away amid all the political problems, and the people working for them, the descendants of the slaves. I hate to even use the word [“slave”], but they took over houses where they worked if somebody was gone for over 10 years. I think people have the right to occupy the house and live there. So this is what the movie is about, and so I spoke at length with both sides – people who went away, whose house was squatted, so to speak, and they had this colonial anger; and the people who squatted, who lived there. It’s very political, and I felt for both sides. So it was important for me to understand both sides. There are always two sides. You recently signed on as executive producer on Rosita Larocca’s directorial debut feature documentary Gia – The Shadow of Beauty , about Gia Carangi (1960–1986). The U.S.-Italy co-production approaches her “not as a pop-cultural icon but as a young woman navigating desire, abandonment and visibility in 1980s New York.” Can you tell me a little bit about what brought you to this project and why you wanted to do that? I was always fascinated by Gia Carangi and her arc in this show business world. She was somebody who was a very smart girl who was not fully inside the system. She was very broken and then had her battles with addiction. And there is also the fact that she was lesbian at a time when that was a huge taboo. So, there are many fascinating [themes and issues] to explore. THR

title: Marc Turtletaub To Direct Feature Adaptation Of Ben Reeves’ Novel ‘Everything Was Beautiful And Nothing Hurt’
full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Marc Turtletaub On His Sprawling Scottish Road Movie ‘Borges and Me’ — Edinburgh Caron Creighton On Capturing The Fight To Save Northern California’s Largest Homeless Encampment With Her Debut Feature ‘Wood Street’ ‘Black Zombie’: Maya Annik Bedward On Her 10-Year Journey To Explore The Political History Of Cinema’s Favorite Monster View All August 13, 2026 1:05am Marc Turtletaub. Miikka Skaffari/Getty Images. EXCLUSIVE: Marc Turtletaub will direct a feature adaptation of Ben Reeves ’ novel Everything Was Beautiful and Nothing Hurt . The novel, which landed on the New York Times Bestsellers List in its first week, will be adapted by screenwriter Oren Moverman. Everything Was Beautiful and Nothing Hurt tells the story of Travis, who lives with his cat in a small, gray town. His job is to offer people comfort in their final hours of life, which he does without complaint or judgment. But when Travis meets Dalia, a midwife, and her boisterous eight-year-old daughter Layla, who live across the hall, he begins to understand what it means to be truly alive—and what might be irrevocably lost in death. Related Stories News Marc Turtletaub On His Sprawling Scottish Road Movie 'Borges and Me' -- Edinburgh News Bleecker Street Bets On Ben Kingsley & 'Jules'; 'The Pod Generation', Stephen King Doc Debut As Strike Keeps Talent On Sidelines - Specialty Preview Moverman and Turtletaub have enjoyed a long-standing creative partnership. Moverman wrote Turtletaub’s 2018 film Puzzle and his latest feature, Borges and Me , which debuts this weekend at the Edinburgh International Film Festival. Watch on Deadline Turtletaub revealed his plans to adapt Reeves’ novel during an interview with Deadline , ahead of his trip to Edinburgh. “The next one is based on a book written by the British author Ben Reeves. It’s called Everything Was Beautiful and Nothing Hurt . It just came out and, in its first week, was on the New York Times bestseller list, so we think it’s quite special,” Turtletaub said, adding the film will be shot in the UK. title: ITN Journalist Exited With “Significant” Payoff After Review Found He Suffered Mental Health Discrimination
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Jenna Fischer Joins Outpouring Of Support For ‘The Office’ Star Lucy Davis After She Revealed Terminal Cancer Diagnosis After Chaos Of Cruise Vs Pitt AI Deepfakes, Seedance 2.5 Is Now Blocking Hollywood Rip-Offs ‘Saturday Night Live UK’ Season 2 Gets Premiere Date View All August 13, 2026 1:00am ITN's headquarters ITN/Matt Freestone EXCLUSIVE : ITN is facing fresh questions about its workplace culture after an external review concluded that a journalist suffered disability discrimination when raising concerns about his working environment, Deadline can reveal. Leo, a pseudonym we are using to protect the identity of the journalist, left ITN in April with a “significant” undisclosed financial settlement after a tumultuous conclusion to his 12-year-long career at the company, where he was once recognized as a rising star and secured Royal Television Society award nominations. ITN is the respected British production outfit behind ITV , Channel 4 and Paramount-owned 5’s news services, as well as hit Netflix documentaries, such as The Investigation of Lucy Letby . But in recent years it has been dogged by questions about its culture, approach to complaints handling, and use of non-disclosure agreements. Related Stories Cancellations and Renewals 'Sorry, I Didn't Know's Historic ITV Run Extends To Seventh Season News ITV's Zandland Doc 'Inside Iran: War & Revolution' Goes Undercover During Anti-Regime Protests & Conflict With The U.S. In 2024, a review by law firm Simmons & Simmons concluded that there was “low trust and psychological safety” within parts of ITN, according to a summary seen by Deadline. Some employees complained that they were reluctant to speak out, fearing that it could impact their wellbeing. Watch on Deadline Leo’s story thrusts these issues back into the spotlight, not least because the external HR consultant engaged by ITN to improve workplace conditions and provide management training was deemed to have discriminated against Leo, albeit unintentionally. ITN said the wellbeing of its employees was “paramount,” and that it investigates concerns fairly and has learned from past mistakes. The company strongly refutes the way the events involving Leo have been characterized, but said it could not comment on individuals. ITN did not admit any liability as part of Leo’s exit agreement, per documents seen by Deadline. Leo, who did not sign an NDA after leaving ITN, has a history of mental health issues. He was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder after reporting on the terror attack on an Ariana Grande concert in Manchester in 2017. Then in 2023, he was signed off work and hospitalized with depression. ITN gave Leo access to trauma support and private therapy, but has admitted to shortcomings in handling his mental health after his 2023 breakdown. This included breaching his privacy in July 2024 when an HR executive shared sensitive information about his condition without Leo’s consent. In interviews with Deadline, Leo said the deterioration of his working relationship with a senior colleague sparked a chain of events that led to his departure, including Leo himself facing a gross misconduct investigation. Deadline is not disclosing the identity of the senior colleague or the ITN division in which Leo worked. Leo alleged that the relationship breakdown was exacerbated by a power imbalance that resulted in him becoming isolated at work. This was disputed by other sources familiar with the situation, who did not recognize the power dynamic described by Leo. The sources added that the relationship breakdown also provoked serious concerns about the wellbeing of the senior colleague. ITN facilities In November 2024, Leo wrote an email to his senior colleague detailing his misgivings about their working relationship, as well as expressing concerns to managers and HR. The correspondence triggered an ITN investigation, which was overseen by a representative from People Puzzles, an external HR consultancy drafted in to improve ITN’s people management and complaints procedures. Leo told ITN he did not want or expect the matters to be formally investigated. He feared that the investigation could be weighted in favor of his colleague because of their seniority, despite receiving assurances that this was not the case. The senior colleague was ultimately cleared of wrongdoing, but Leo claimed that the investigation was flawed because of its focus on his mental illness. Leo Subject To “Disadvantages” His subsequent complaint about ITN’s investigation was examined as part of an external review by Kane HR, per a report seen by Deadline. Kane HR concluded that the ITN’s investigation “inappropriately strayed” into a discussion about Leo’s mental wellbeing and its impact on the workplace, instead of focusing on fact-finding. “My view is that [the] employee was subjected to some disadvantages in the investigation process, based on his disability, and it could have been conducted in a fairer and more conciliatory way,” the report said. Kane HR concluded that Leo’s experience was “discriminatory,” though stressed that this was not done intentionally and that no “statutory requirements” were breached by the People Puzzles consultant. The Kane HR report said the original investigation’s recommendations were “comprehensive and reasonable,” but added that there were elements of Leo’s experience that “may have been appropriate to investigate further.” Leo submitted his written statement after the original investigation had closed, telling ITN he was too unwell to meet earlier deadlines set by the People Puzzles consultant. Kane HR said another deadline extension would have been a “reasonable adjustment” given the “knowledge of his ill health.” Once the statement was received, the People Puzzles consultant’s view was that it did not change the outcome of the investigation, which absolved the senior colleague. ITN stands by the findings of the original investigation, despite admitting that the process was flawed. In a June 2025 email to Leo, ITN’s general counsel Zaffrin O’Sullivan wrote: “The company accepts the findings set out in the report and acknowledges and apologises for the instances in which [Kane HR] has found that the original investigation fell short of the standards which you were entitled to expect having raised concerns.” She later told him that it was a “red line” moment for ITN, according to Leo. People Puzzles, which did not respond to a request for comment, is no longer engaged by ITN. Leo Launches Lawsuit; ITN Opens Probe After the investigations, ITN and Leo established a framework for his continued employment, but he argued that the arrangements diluted his role and responsibilities, leaving him isolated and vulnerable to losing his job. Leo’s former co-workers told Deadline that it was a complex situation for all involved. These ITN insiders said the relationship breakdown, and subsequent working framework, created confusion about responsibilities and was difficult to navigate. In December 2025, Leo filed an employment tribunal lawsuit against ITN, claiming discrimination arising from his disability. Within weeks, the company launched its own investigation into Leo’s conduct, citing concerns that he went on a reporting assignment without permission, published an article on Substack without approval, and made a comment to a manager that was perceived as a threat to report his superior to HR. The review concluded that Leo’s actions amounted to gross misconduct and he would face disciplinary action, according to a document seen by Deadline. Leo denied wrongdoing and told Deadline that the investigation felt like a retaliatory “fishing expedition” designed to gather evidence ahead of a potential legal battle. Leo claimed that he was not allowed to call his own witnesses as part of an investigation, which ITN insiders dispute, even though all those interviewed were his superiors. Leo added that he was never shown the terms of reference and the investigation report made no substantive allowances for his mental health or previous experience of discrimination. In a letter to ITN, Leo’s therapist said the investigation had a “profound psychological” impact on the journalist. “Where an individual already experiences the workplace as unsafe, unsupportive, or punitive after raising concerns, the escalation of formal processes can be profoundly destabilising,” she added. Leo’s attorney argued that the ITN investigation was a “further act of discrimination” and was evidence that his working relationship had “irretrievably broken down,” per a letter seen by Deadline. Proposing an exit deal that would involve Leo dropping his lawsuit, the lawyer added: “My client cannot now, in good conscience, remain in a working environment that is making him unwell and poses further risk to his mental health.” Leo left in April with an undisclosed payoff as part of an agreement that settled his lawsuit, but he has continued to raise concerns about his experience. “I just wouldn’t want anyone else to go through this,” Leo told Deadline. “I believed in [ITN], and I believed in its journalistic principles. It was my dream place to work and to then have the experience that I had was just beyond devastating.” ITN insiders shared concerns about the company’s HR processes, but they told Deadline that it would have been a complex situation to navigate, even for an extremely skilled and experienced people management professional. An ITN spokesperson told Deadline: “When a concern is raised we consider it promptly, thoroughly and fairly in view of everyone involved. The wellbeing of all our staff is paramount, and where shortcomings to HR processes have been identified in the past we have learnt from them and always seek continual improvement. While we strongly refute the way these events have been characterised, it would not be appropriate to comment on individuals.” Claudia-Liza Vanderpuije ITN’s culture was a subject of discussion in UK Parliament in March 2025. MP Layla Moran used parliamentary privilege to tell the story of a female employee, who was allegedly suspended after complaining about a “coercive, controlling sexual relationship with an older male editor.” Moran claimed that the woman was prevented from speaking about her experience because of an NDA. More recently, former 5 News presenter Claudia-Liza Vanderpuije sued ITN over allegations of sexism, racial harassment, unfair dismissal, and suffering a detriment due to exercising her whistleblowing rights. The case was settled before going to court, with ITN denying wrongdoing. ITN has since installed Ian Rumsey as its new CEO, replacing Rachel Corp in May. The company’s HR team has also been restructured following the Simmons & Simmons review, while internal employee resources for reporting concerns have been strengthened. title: Marc Turtletaub On His Sprawling Scottish Road Movie ‘Borges and Me’ — Edinburgh
full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Marc Turtletaub On His Sprawling Scottish Road Movie ‘Borges and Me’ — Edinburgh Caron Creighton On Capturing The Fight To Save Northern California’s Largest Homeless Encampment With Her Debut Feature ‘Wood Street’ ‘Black Zombie’: Maya Annik Bedward On Her 10-Year Journey To Explore The Political History Of Cinema’s Favorite Monster View All August 13, 2026 1:00am Veteran director-producer Marc Turtletaub returns to feature filmmaking this year with Borges and Me , which screens this weekend in one of the primetime Out of Competition spots at the Edinburgh International Film Festival. Directed by Turtletaub from a screenplay by Oren Moverman, the film follows a young graduate student at the University of St Andrews who embarks on the trip of a lifetime across the Scottish Highlands accompanied by the legendary poet Jorge Luis Borges. The picture is an adaptation of Jay Parini’s popular memoir Borges and Me: An Encounter . Fionn Whitehead and Luis Gnecco lead the film alongside a band of popular Scottish actors, including Alan Cumming, Freya Mavor, John Gordon Sinclair, Morven Christie, Peter Mullan, and Stuart Bowman. Check out a clip from the feature above, and below, you can read our interview with Turtletaub ahead of this weekend’s screenings in Edinburgh. Turtletaub discusses how he stumbled upon Parini’s best-selling novel and how he mounted this large-scale production in 61 locations across Scotland. Turtletaub also teases his next feature project. Related Stories News Supernatural Thriller 'Snapshot' Gets Sales Deal Ahead Of Edinburgh & Frightfest Bows, Watch First Clip Festivals 'Mission' Clip: George MacKay & Rosy McEwen Lead Edinburgh Competition Title DEADLINE: Marc, how did this project come to be? Where did you find the book? MARC TURTLETAUB: We have book scouts. We have other producers send us material. We develop our own. But this one I just found in a bookstore. I was actually on vacation in Hawaii, walked into a bookstore, and saw it. The book was a few years old at that point and looked interesting. I knew a little bit about Borges, but not as much as I do now. I started reading it and fell in love with it. DEADLINE: In all those years, did no one else try to adapt the book? It feels like a ready-made story. TURTLETAUB: There was another team that had tried to put it together, but it hadn’t happened, so they were open to us coming and getting involved. It’s a road movie, so the first thing I did, even before we had the rights to the book, was get in a car and drive from St Andrews up to Orkney. I took the exact route from the book and tried to stay in all the same places. As we were going, I would identify possible shooting locations. DEADLINE: This is a road movie, and it’s rare for films of this scale to be made in the UK. Was it a difficult process to build this production? TURTLETAUB : We make our own movies and then sell them, so we have that big advantage. The film was a co-production between four countries: Holland, Belgium, the UK, and the U.S., so we had an interesting mix of financing. But you’re right, these kinds of movies are rare these days. But we had a great line producer who introduced us to the best crew in Scotland, and having these great Scottish actors join made it a real pleasure. DEADLINE: Yes, this is a great cast. Luis, who plays Borges, is amazing. I believe he is from Chile? TURTLETAUB : Yes, Luis Gnecco. He starred in Neruda , the film about Pablo Neruda, so he seems to specialize in these great writers. I fell in love with his work. He was probably the best-prepared actor I have ever worked with. He read just about everything that had been written about Borges. He found a movie that I didn’t even know existed, which Borges had written. He saw live interviews with Borges. He met someone who knew Borges and interviewed him. In the script, there is a line where Borges says something in Anglo-Saxon, so Luis learned Anglo-Saxon. So that’s the guy that showed up, truly marrying talent with preparation. He was a real treat. And then Fionn Whitehead, who was the lead in Dunkirk , was great as a foil to this wild Luis Gnecco. And then we were able to get all these great Scottish actors: Alan Cumming, Peter Mullan, Freya Mavor, people that were signing on because they liked the project, and we were quite fortunate. DEADLINE: How involved was Jay in the production? TURTLETAUB : He loves filmmaking, and we welcomed him. He was on set every day. In fact, one day we were shooting the scene where Freya Mavor sings a song. Jay was there and, within an hour, wrote the lyrics. So he was a great supporter. The screenplay was written by Oren Moverman, who is a good friend. Oren wrote another movie I made called Puzzle , and he’s going to be working on the next one that I’m going to make. So we have a good relationship. When Jay read the screenplay, he said to Oren, “This is a masterclass in adaptation.” So we knew he liked it, which was important to us. DEADLINE: What’s the next one going to be? TURTLETAUB : The next one is based on a book written by the British author Ben Reeves. It’s called Everything Was Beautiful and Nothing Hurt . It just came out and, in its first week, was on the New York Times bestseller list, so we think it’s quite special. DEADLINE: Marc, you’ve done a lot in your filmmaking career. Is there anything left that you’d like to tick off your list? TURTLETAUB : We really love what we’re doing. I want to continue doing it well. I’ve been able to pass on the leadership of our company to Tim Foley and Michael Clark, and that feels great because one is my son and the other feels like my nephew. We’ve worked together for almost 20 years. And we’re looking at new things as a company. We’re working on a low-cost 3D animation, and we’re excited about that. That’ll be something new for us. This past year we shot an independent TV pilot without a distributor, with Nicole Holofcener directing. It’s called Worried and follows two sisters living in New York. We’re looking forward to lining up a distribution for that. So those are two new things the company is doing, and for me, it’s just about continuing to do what I’m doing and helping support the next generation. title: ‘The Wrong Girls’ Review: Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat Are a Good Time in Dylan Meyer’s Shaggy Stoner Comedy
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 13, 2026 12:47am PT ‘The Wrong Girls’ Review: Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat Are a Good Time in Dylan Meyer’s Shaggy Stoner Comedy Following two burnout friends on an absurd LA quest, the writer-director's debut feature aims for late-night cult status and might well get it. By Katie Walsh Plus Icon Katie Walsh Latest See All Courtesy of Neon Debut writer-director Dylan Meyer practically achieves liftoff with her absurdist stoner comedy “ The Wrong Girls ,” starring Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat . If Method Man and Red Man once posited “How High” with their 2001 comedy, Meyer counters with a pair of pals who achieve psychic powers through experimental psychedelics. And while Dave Chappelle was “Half Baked” in 1998, put a fork in Frankie (Stewart) and Molly (Shawkat), because they’re fully done. The burnout duo, who live in an LA apartment dubbed Casa de Chill Zone, put Cheech and Chong to shame with their reefer madness. Related Stories 'Baywatch' Swims to Prime Video in Canada, Latin America, India and Europe AI-Generated Turkish Series 'Castle Walls' Launches on Prime Video in What Is Being Touted as a Worldwide Streaming First – Trailer (EXCLUSIVE) Meyer blends together almost a few too many familiar strains for the plot of “The Wrong Girls,” which takes a minute to gain coherence before almost immediately losing it again. In this crazy California yarn, Frankie and Molly have to come up with rent money by the next day, as in F. Gary Gray’s 1995 LA stoner classic “Friday” (as well as last year’s “One of Them Days”), a quest that sends them on an odyssey fit for “Harold and Kumar Go to White Castle.” Meanwhile, a mistaken identity twist has a mercenary nicknamed Not Metal Head Dave (LaKeith Stanfield) and a team of Danish scientists and security contractors hot on their heels. Squid brains, talking cats and telepathy, oh my! Popular on Variety It may be loosey-goosey, but Meyer’s film is far from a bad trip. The ensemble cast is especially charming, and the good humor oozing out of the entire project means it’s hard to avoid a contact high. Stewart and Shawkat have a fun and amiable vibe together, even if their characters aren’t immediately in focus. Frankie is a Stanford engineering student who failed out of college and now works as a “Kwik Things” delivery driver. Codependent bestie Molly is a weed-inspired aspiring chef whose utterly reasonable boyfriend Josh (Zack Fox) would really love for her to get her life together and move in with him. Frankie, on the other hand, discovers that her latest beau Mike Z. (Morgan Krantz) has replaced her with a straitlaced doppelgänger upgrade, Frances (Stewart in glasses). At a Mannequin Pussy show, she confronts the pair, then runs into the aforementioned Not Metal Head Dave, who passes her a secretive briefcase, thinking that Frankie is high-level researcher Frances. Which is how Frankie and Molly find themselves in possession of some seriously heady psychedelics derived from deep sea squid testes. They make themselves unwitting test subjects for the stuff before trying to sell the drugs at a Stanford alumni event hosted by Martin (Tony Hale), and suddenly find themselves highly valuable assets for the drug researchers, including Dr. Olsen (Kate McKinnon), when it’s discovered they’ve gained telepathic powers during their trip. McKinnon is a comedic MVP as always, and Stanfield proves himself again to be a Swiss Army knife as a performer, ably fitting into any genre, role or ensemble cast, and demonstrating both comic chemistry with McKinnon and sexual chemistry with Stewart (one-sided on her part). Seth Rogen and Kumail Nanjiani voice Frankie and Molly’s cats to great effect. A Geena Davis cameo reminds us of another great film about female friendship, “Thelma & Louise,” though this one has a happier ending. Cinematographer Todd Banhazl achieves the ‘90s retro druggie look with a brightly saturated palette, hazy filtered light, Dutch angles and wide lenses, while rocker-turned-composer Ty Segall lays down some nasty psych-surf rock guitar licks on the score — though some of the twangy flourishes get a touch repetitive. “The Wrong Girls” feels heavy on inside humor, much of it LA-centric — jokes about freeways, anyone? But Meyer is generous enough to want to bring the audience in on it, and she does make tangible her references. Those not in SoCal might not quite get the depths of the bit about Frankie and Molly mourning a restaurant called “Souper Starz Buffet” (R.I.P. Souplantation), but Meyer makes their tearful goodbye, and final feast, palpably emotional and fun to watch. It all feels like a cult hit in a good way: the kind of movie you’d watch over and over on Comedy Central or on DVD because it’s just so silly, a little rough around the edges, but highly specific. It seems like that’s exactly what Meyer was going for too, so if that’s your thing, light it up and pass that Dutch. ‘The Wrong Girls’ Review: Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat Are a Good Time in Dylan Meyer’s Shaggy Stoner Comedy Reviewed at Wilshire Screening Room, Los Angeles, Aug. 11, 2026. title: Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market Names Japan 2026 Focus Country for Producer Hub
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 13, 2026 12:21am PT Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market Names Japan 2026 Focus Country for Producer Hub By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest BTS’ V Reveals Hearing Loss Amid World Tour 1 hour ago Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market Names Japan 2026 Focus Country for Producer Hub 3 hours ago Indian Freedom Fighter Bhagat Singh Series in Development at Collective Studios’ Historyverse (EXCLUSIVE) 7 hours ago See All Busan ACFM The Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) has selected Japan as the 2026 Focus Country for its Producer Hub, a co-production networking platform tied to the Busan International Film Festival . Japan will send 10 producers to Busan in October for project pitching, speed meetings and case-study sessions. Now in its third year, Producer Hub gives producers pursuing international co-productions a forum to trade information and build relationships. The initiative singles out one focus country annually, using the selection to showcase that market’s production landscape, incentive programs and slate of in-development projects. Related Stories American Film Market Expands With Launch of AFM House, Site of Its Innovation Hub 'The Traitors' India Sets August Season 2 Bow on Prime Video (EXCLUSIVE) This year’s Japanese delegation will pitch active co-production projects, detail how the country’s production system operates and look for new partners across the region, according to ACFM. Popular on Variety ACFM launched Producer Hub in 2024 as a dedicated space for producers to compare notes on financing, investment and local support schemes across different territories. Korea held the inaugural focus country slot in 2024, co-hosted by the Korean Film Council. Canada took the spot in 2025 alongside Telefilm Canada, an edition that drew 154 producers representing 25 countries. That exchange takes on added significance following an audiovisual co-production treaty Canada and the Korea signed in 2026, which organizers expect will deepen ties between the two countries. Producer Hub’s partner network has meanwhile grown from eight organizations in seven countries at launch to 13 organizations across 10 countries today. Producer Hub 2026 runs four days, from Oct. 10 to 13 – one day longer than the 2025 edition. The Japanese delegation will pitch in-development projects and detail the country’s production environment, while separate case-study sessions will examine past co-productions between Japan and other countries. Speed meetings and networking sessions round out the schedule. Organizers added the extra day to give participants more room to build on early conversations. Follow-up sessions are being arranged specifically with the Japanese producers so that discussions started during speed meetings can continue, moving past introductions into details on projects, production conditions and potential collaboration, according to ACFM. ACFM Director Ellen Y.D. Kim said, “Japan today is Asia’s most dynamic co-production partner. Building on its longstanding strength in independent and arthouse cinema, international collaboration is expanding on all fronts to encompass commercial films and series, backed by bold policies centered on grants and incentives,” adding, “Together with Japan, this year’s focus country, Producer Hub aims to serve as a platform offering producers across Asia tangible opportunities for collaboration.” Producer Hub plans to keep expanding its roster of partner organizations beyond the current 13 across 10 countries. Producers interested in international co-production can apply via the ACFM website, with the application window open through Aug. 31. ACFM runs in Busan each October alongside BIFF. The market’s 20th edition in 2025 was its largest yet, with registration reaching 1,222 companies and 3,024 professionals across 55 countries and total on-site attendance hitting 30,006. Its Sales Market logged 8,438 business meetings, with a transaction value estimated at $71.1 million. The 2026 Asian Contents & Film Market runs Oct. 10–13 at BEXCO’s Exhibition Center 2 in Busan, alongside the 31st Busan International Film Festival, set for Oct. 6–15. title: ‘Far From the Trees’ Director Meritxell Colell on Turning Exile and Endangered Languages Into a ‘Body of Memory’
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 12, 2026 10:22pm PT ‘Far From the Trees’ Director Meritxell Colell on Turning Exile and Endangered Languages Into a ‘Body of Memory’ By Callum McLennan Plus Icon Callum McLennan Latest Edinburgh Industry Program Features Ewan McGregor, Kenneth Branagh and Bruce Dern and an Inaugural U.K. Film Conference 3 weeks ago ‘Cowboy’ Director Nathan Grubbs on Betting the Farm to Make His Louisiana Western 4 weeks ago Canary Islands’ Documentary Voices Look Outward as Sector Gains Range 2 months ago See All In “Far From the Trees,” (“Lejos de los árboles”) Meritxell Colell asks viewers to listen before they try to understand. Premiering in Locarno’s international competition, the Spain-Italy-Peru production from Allegra Films follows Adela, a 50-year-old Mexican sound artist who travels from the Peruvian jungle to the Andes recording endangered languages. Accompanied by a guide and translator, she is continuing the work of her grandfather, a Catalan Republican exiled in Mexico. But news of her grandmother’s possible death fractures the journey, drawing Adela into childhood memories, family silences and fantastical visions. Related Stories Inside Netflix and Prime Video’s Fight to Reshape France’s Streaming Rules: 'It's an Unsustainable Equation' 'Baywatch' Swims to Prime Video in Canada, Latin America, India and Europe For the director, the film began with an absence. Popular on Variety “‘Lejos de los árboles’ came into being in 2020 following the death of a very close family member. At the time, I knew only that I wanted to address the inability to say goodbye—the inability to view a dead body and the emotions that entails—and to link this to sound,” Colell told Variety. She initially searched for displaced or migrant sound artists and encountered Angélica Castelló, a Mexico-born, Vienna-based composer whose grandfather had also gone into exile. “The film emerged from her story and those initial impulses; years later, I realized it also connected deeply with my own life – specifically, with the legacy of silence passed down by my grandparents,” Colell explained. Rather than reconstructing her own family history directly, she created Adela: a fictional figure whose identity is formed by migration, artistic vocation and the simple fact of being often elsewhere. “I was determined to center the film on the complexity of hybrid identities shaped by exile and migration –identities where the status of ‘foreigner’ becomes the self – and on the burden of that inheritance,” she said. The geographical distance was crucial. Adela follows her grandfather’s footsteps while transforming his political and anthropological work into art, weaving a sound map from languages at risk of disappearing. The connection between Indigenous languages in Peru and Catalan exile was not part of the earliest drafts, but became the idea that brought the film into focus. “Once the idea of vulnerable languages came up, everything fell into place,” said Colell. “It became clear that her work was carrying on her grandfather’s legacy, adding a new dimension to his figure.” The grandfather became an activist-anthropologist dedicated to recovering native languages in Mexico, a calling linked to his flight from a Catalonia where Franco’s regime suppressed languages other than Castillian Spanish. “In a way, the film is an ode to the beauty of languages, to their collective value, and to multilingualism as a viable social reality,” Colell says. “Language is a form of thought, a way of seeing and inhabiting the world. We don’t necessarily have to understand every form; we simply need to listen to them, however we can.” That principle shapes the film itself. We hear the birds, wind, voices, music, the whirr of a grandmother’s sewing machine and a thud against a trunk of a tree. “Sound is essential in cinema – not only on narrative and contextual levels but also on perceptual and emotional ones,” observed Colell. “That is why I was so eager to make a film featuring a sound artist as the protagonist.” The film’s Super 16mm passages, which inhabit memories, visions and reveries, were shot without synchronized sound. The voices of Adela’s grandparents and Paula were recorded separately, leaving Castelló free to build what Colell calls “a sonic tapestry woven from a multitude of sounds.” Castelló’s presence reshaped the film over years of residencies, meetings and debate. The director was determined, however, that Adela would firmly be fictional rather than becoming a portrait of the performer. “It was a way to lighten the role, turn it into a game, and distance it from reality,” she said. “It was crucial for me to portray a person in her fifties who had left her home country to pursue her passion– music – and to depict a type of woman rarely seen on screen.” “As time went on, my initial intuition upon meeting her was confirmed: She was the film.” Producer Mayca Sanz L-Higueras began assembling the project in 2021, initially seeking a European structure that could connect with Latin America through Ibermedia. Italy’s Exit Media joined first; Peru’s Animalita Cine later came on board, while RTVE helped complete the financing. “In Peru, the biggest challenge has been finding someone willing to commit to filming with a fiction crew – albeit a very small one – in a country completely unprepared for such a project, and with a story that required the commitment of non-professional actors whom the director had sought out, selected and worked with over time, following location scouting trips spanning three years,” said Sanz. The shoot unfolded in five blocks over more than a year, beginning in February 2024 and ending with Teresita Sánchez’s scenes in July 2025. Colell also became a mother during production. “At times, I worried that shooting in such fragmented stages might result in something of a Frankenstein’s monster; I’m used to filming in chronological order,” she says. “The surprise came when we started editing and saw that everything actually fit together perfectly.” For Allegra Films, Locarno’s selection validates a leap into a more ambitious international model. For Colell, it offers a setting suited to a film that resists tidy explanations. “I love open cinema– films that engage the viewer and connect them to their own lived experience. Cinema that pierces you and settles deep in your gut, beneath your skin, in your chest,” she says. She hopes younger viewers will leave the screening wanting to investigate the history of exile, or to ask their own relatives what was never said. “The film speaks to the need to listen, the importance of passing things on, and how we people act as both transmitters and receivers of memory,” said Colell. “And, in a sense, the film itself is a body of memory.” The collaboration between director and lead allows “Far From the Trees” to examine the cost of building a life elsewhere. Adela’s strained relationship with those tasked with caring for her grandmother, raises questions about who stays, who leaves and who inherits responsibility. “Distance is inherently complicated, yet it can also be liberating,” said Colell. “I wanted to explore this issue without judgment: to discuss the consequences of living far from family, how that shapes one’s identity, and how it affects those who take on caregiving duties.” She recalls Castelló telling her: “I am a permanent foreigner. My home – my refuge – is sound. Music.” “That statement encapsulates the film’s central quest,” Colell concludes. “I would love for the film itself to become that home, that refuge.” Ricky Gervais’ Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Alley Cats’ Is Surprisingly Bittersweet: TV Review Loading comments... title: Ritchie Blackmore Performs With Deep Purple for First Time Since Acrimonious Split in Early ’90s, After Warning Fans: ‘I Have Not Played Rock Music in 25 Years’
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 12, 2026 9:27pm PT Ritchie Blackmore Performs With Deep Purple for First Time Since Acrimonious Split in Early ’90s, After Warning Fans: ‘I Have Not Played Rock Music in 25 Years’ By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Ritchie Blackmore Performs With Deep Purple for First Time Since Acrimonious Split in Early ’90s, After Warning Fans: ‘I Have Not Played Rock Music in 25 Years’ 6 hours ago The Band Perry’s Family Feud Lights Up: Neil Perry Says He Was ‘Terminated’ From Sibling Trio, as Kimberly Perry’s Husband Stepped In to Make It a Marital Duo 16 hours ago Kennedy Center Ordered to Pay $250,000 to Jazz Musician It Unsuccessfully Sued for Backing Out of Concert After Trump Rebranding 2 days ago See All Universal Archive/Universal Imag Most Deep Purple fans had long since given up any hope of seeing the band ever share a stage with founding guitarist Ritchie Blackmore again, due to a well-know, decades-long estrangement. But that’s exactly what took place near the end of the group’s show Wednesday night at Jones Beach in New York, as hatchets were buried and Blackmore rejoined his old mates for a rendition of the group’s most famous song, “Smoke on the Water.” “It’s gonna be interesting,” Blackmore said in a podcast appearance the night before the show, in which the 81-year-old guitar legend leaked news of his imminent appearance. “i have not played rock music in 25 years.” Related Stories Errol Spence, Jr. vs. Tim Tszyu Livestream: Here's Where to Watch the Middleweight Pay-Per-View Match Online 'Baywatch' Swims to Prime Video in Canada, Latin America, India and Europe At the conclusion of “Smoke in the Water” Wednesday, singer Ian Gillan showered praise on his ex-bandmate before he left the stage. “A couple of days ago I got a message from a local lad… saying ‘I only live around the corner, do you mind if I come and jam with you?’ It was an absolute pleasure to have back on stage the founding member, the great legend,”the immortal Ritchie Blackmore. Thanks, Ritchie. i have to say, it was a great pleasure. I’ll see you in the bar.” Popular on Variety Probably few in the audience were taken by complete surprise by Blackmore’s cameo, since the previous night, the guitarist had spilled some of the beans in a livestream conversation with his wife, singer Candice Night, the evening before the Jones Beach gig. Blackmore said on Tuesday’s live podcast that he was revealing the secret in advance because he wanted fans who had waited for this moment for decades to at least have a shot at making it to New York in time for Wednesday’s show. Blackmore, who co-founded Deep Purple in 1968, had a fallout with other members in 1993 that resulted in him leaving the lineup in 1993 for the second and last time. The fallout was bad enough that Blackmore did not show up at the band’s Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction in 2016, after being told that the currently touring lineup — which still includes three original or near-original members in Gillan, drummer Ian Paice and bassist Roger Glover — would not reunite with him under any circumstances, even for a short, one-off performance at the ceremony. So hell seemed to have frozen over when Gillan recently sent a message gingerly asking if he could come up on stage for one number at a tour date… and the band proved surprisingly agreeable to that notion, after so much water under the bridge. “it is a secret and i don’t want anybody to know, but I’m probably going to go up and do an encore with the band, Deep Purple,” Blackmore blurted about eight minutes into the livestream with his wife, singer Candice Night. “But you can’t tell anybody, and I know this will be kept a secret. won’t it?” he joked, even as the web lit up with the news quickly being spread among hard rock buffs. Blackmore explained the genesis of this unexpected reunion: “I sent my AI pigeon to Ian Gillan in Portugal, where he lives at the moment, and I said, ‘How would you feel if I got up just for an encore on one of the songs. Don’t want to intrude.’ And I said, ‘No pressure, just kind of old times’ sake.’ You know, I’m 81 now. So (Gillan) seemed to li0e the idea, put it to the band, got a thumbs up, and it looks like we might be doing that.” The guitarist admitted he was hardly in practice for a performance with Deep Purple, given the drift in his musical focus since 1993, as he moved on to gentler brand of folk-rock with Blackmore’s Night, the band fronted by his wife. “I changed my strings on my Strat, which i haven’t done in over 25 years,” he revealed. “It’s kind of frightening. I haven’t played rock in 25 years. I’ve been playing acoustic guitar for 25 years. And at first i was very uncomfortable playing (acoustic guitar), but i got used to it, and now I’m more used to playing the acoustic, more so than the electric.” He said he needed some medical assistance in being able to withstand “Smoke on the Water.” “I did have my injection in my lumbar area yesterday,” he explained on the podcast, of needing a steroid shot. “it’s a special injection i have that enables me to stand in one spot, because if I’m playing a Strat, i have a hard time… I have four herniated discs, if anybody wants them. And I had my injection yesterday of a steroid which helps me get through standing on stage. But I have kind of a stool there, just in case I start toppling over or something.” Of his reasons for giving fans 24 hours’ notice, he said he “wanted to warn the people living in Romania, so they could fly over… Not really. I just thought it might be an idea to let a few people know because I think a lot of people would like to see that.” what a moment in time… pic.twitter.com/tTOq2RUXP6 — Candice Night (@TruCandiceNight) August 13, 2026 His announcement of sitting in with the group concluded with the thoughts: “I hope people enjoy it.” And: “it will be good to see the old guys again.” well, this warms my heart… pic.twitter.com/2nArOmSihz — Candice Night (@TruCandiceNight) August 13, 2026 Fans from afar turned to the web to look for footage of the show. Perrin Wolfson and Jimmy Kay of the Metal Voice podcast livestreame through the latter part of Deep Purple’s set, waiting for confirmation that it had gone down, and putting up photos and video that were shared with them from inside the show. “History has been made,” Wolfson and Kay crowed as they first got word “Smoke in the Water” was in progress with Blackmore aboard. “I feel like we just walked on the moon.” Ricky Gervais’ Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Alley Cats’ Is Surprisingly Bittersweet: TV Review Loading comments... title: Andreas Dresen, Doris Dörrie Films to World Premiere  at Zurich Film Festival
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 12, 2026 9:00pm PT Andreas Dresen, Doris Dörrie Films to World Premiere at Zurich Film Festival By Leo Barraclough Plus Icon Leo Barraclough International Features Editor LeoBarraclough Latest Andreas Dresen, Doris Dörrie Films to World Premiere at Zurich Film Festival 6 hours ago 1-2 Special Takes U.S. Rights to Michal Marczak’s Sundance Documentary ‘Closure’ (EXCLUSIVE) 19 hours ago Oscar Nominee Barkhad Abdi, Jim Deddes Lead Teddy Cherim’s ‘Maalstroom’; First-Look Image Released (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago See All "Love, After All" (Courtesy of Andres Dresen, Kordes und Kordes Film, Pandora) The world premieres of two major German films, Andreas Dresen ’s “Love, After All” and Doris Dörrie ’s “How Can I Help?,” are among 11 titles to feature in the Gala Premieres section of Zurich Film Festival . The selection also includes Oscar contenders “I Play Rocky” and “Josephine,” and Switzerland’s most anticipated film, “111 – Echoes From Halifax.” Christian Jungen, CEO of the festival, said the section is “dedicated to auteur cinema for a broader audience.” Related Stories 'The Legend of Kitchen Soldier,' 'Yumi's Cells' Lead Prime Video India's Slate of 100-Plus New CJ ENM Titles 'Baywatch' Swims to Prime Video in Canada, Latin America, India and Europe “We are particularly delighted that two major figures of German auteur cinema, Andreas Dresen and Doris Dörrie, have entrusted us with the world premieres of their new films,” Jungen said. “Their films are grounded in everyday life and, with a little wink, reflect on the state of our society.” Popular on Variety He added, “We present films that will play an important role later in the award season, such as ‘I Play Rocky.’” The film tells the story behind the making of the cult classic starring Sylvester Stallone, which won the Academy Award for best picture in 1977. Jungen explained that, from a Swiss perspective, “111 – Echoes From Halifax” deserves special mention. “From multiple perspectives, the film sheds light on a major event that shook our nation: the crash of a Swissair aircraft near Halifax,” he said. The full program of the 22nd Zurich Film Festival, which runs Sept. 24 to Oct. 4, will be revealed on Sept. 9. I PLAY ROCKY European Premiere Biography U.S., 2026 Director: Peter Farrelly Cast: Anthony Ippolito, Matt Dillon, Stephan James, AnnaSophia Robb, PJ Byrne, Toby Kebbell, Tracy Letts, Jay Duplass Unknown actor Sylvester Stallone is writing a screenplay titled “Rocky” that a studio is desperate to acquire. But Stallone refuses to sell the rights – unless he gets to play the lead himself. Despite numerous setbacks and rejections, he remains determined to make his dream a reality: playing Rocky Balboa. The result is the ultimate underdog story behind the legendary underdog film. JOSEPHINE Drama U.S., 2026 Director: Beth de Araújo Cast: Channing Tatum, Gemma Chan, Mason Lily Reeves When 8-year-old Josephine witnesses a violent crime, her world is out of joint. She is trying to find a way to regain a sense of security. While her emphatic mother (Gemma Chan) wants to help her process what happened, her father (Channing Tatum) believes in preparing Josephine for the harsher realities of life but increasingly finds himself overwhelmed by the situation. With the suspense of a thriller, director Beth de Araújo tells a deeply empathetic family drama about fear and the limits of parental care. Channing Tatum gives one of his strongest performances in this year’s great Sundance Film Festival sensation. WICKER Comedy U.S., 2025 Director: Alex Huston Fischer, Eleanor Wilson Cast: Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård, Peter Dinklage, Elizabeth Debicki, Marli Siu, Nabhaan Rizwan An audacious comedic fable about sex, marriage and the absurdities of social convention, “Wicker” tells the wholly original love story of an ostracized fisherwoman (Colman) who commissions a husband to be made by the local basketmaker (Dinklage). title: Indian Freedom Fighter Bhagat Singh Series in Development at Collective Studios’ Historyverse (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Aug 12, 2026 8:30pm PT Indian Freedom Fighter Bhagat Singh Series in Development at Collective Studios’ Historyverse (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Drishyam’ Producer Panorama Studios Invests in Indian Vertical Streaming Platform Rocket Reels (EXCLUSIVE) 39 minutes ago BTS’ V Reveals Hearing Loss Amid World Tour 1 hour ago Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market Names Japan 2026 Focus Country for Producer Hub 3 hours ago See All Collective Studios A new original series exploring the life of Indian freedom fighter Bhagat Singh is in development at Collective Studios’ Historyverse . The project is being made in association with Hathiramani Commercial Ventures and co-produced with investor and entrepreneur Manish Hathiramani, who marks his producing debut with the show. The series is designed to move past the familiar episodes of Singh’s story and instead examine the man beneath the myth – his childhood, intellectual development and the social and political forces that shaped his convictions in early 20th-century India. Rather than revisiting the widely known chapters of Singh’s life, the show will track how his ideas evolved across the different stages of his journey, culminating in the revolutionary figure whose legacy continues to endure. Related Stories Errol Spence, Jr. vs. Tim Tszyu Livestream: Here's Where to Watch the Middleweight Pay-Per-View Match Online 'The Traitors' India Sets August Season 2 Bow on Prime Video (EXCLUSIVE) Sudeep Lahiri, head of channels and distribution at Collective Media Network, said: “There are some figures in our history whose stories we think we know completely. Bhagat Singh is one of them. But behind the icon was a young man whose ideas, influences and experiences shaped the person he would become. That is the story we are interested in exploring. Having Manish come on board as a co-producer makes this collaboration particularly exciting, because we share a strong belief in finding new perspectives within stories that have already been told many times and bringing them to audiences with scale and ambition.” Popular on Variety “Bhagat Singh is a figure whose life has always fascinated me, but what interests me most is the person before the legend,” Hathiramani added. “We know the revolutionary, the freedom fighter and the icon; this series gives us an opportunity to understand the many facets of Bhagat Singh’s life and the journey that shaped him. I am delighted to be producing this project with Historyverse and to bring a fresh perspective on his life and legacy to audiences.” Title, cast and additional details are to be confirmed. Singh has been the subject of at least five Indian features, among them “Shaheed” (1965), “Shaheed-E-Azam” (2002), “23rd March 1931: Shaheed” (2002), “The Legend of Bhagat Singh” (2002) and “Rang De Basanti” (2006). The Bhagat Singh project joins a Historyverse slate that already encompasses titles drawn from Indian mythology and history, including projects centered on Shivaji and Swami Samarth. title: ‘The Matrix’ Director Lilly Wachowski Says Hollywood Won’t Finance New Film With Trans Cast
full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 12, 2026 8:25pm Lilly Wachowski Jason Mendez/Getty Images for Tribeca Festival Lilly Wachowski , who co-directed The Matrix franchise, is opening up about the struggle to get financing for her new film that features a “wall-to-wall trans cast.” During a recent interview on KCRW’s The Business podcast , the filmmaker acknowledged that it’s unfortunately “not the greatest time in the industry to be trying to make these kinds of things because all of these opportunities are dwindling for folks with those kinds of stories to tell,” specifically those with “underrepresented voices and marginalized points of view.” Related Stories TV Lilly Wachowski's Anarchists United Sets Writers Discovery Fellows Amid Shifting Hollywood Landscape: "Making Television Looks Very Different" Movies Lilly Wachowski Shares Advice to Her Pre-Transition Self at 'Bound' Reunion Screening: "Start Taking That Estrogen" Wachowski used her next project, The Hunted , as an example, saying it’s been a challenge because when she showed the script around Hollywood, nobody wanted to finance the dystopian political thriller that’s budgeted at roughly $10 million. “People like it, but they really don’t want to make it because it’s [got a] wall-to-wall trans cast,” she said of the film. “I have to get creative and figure out different ways that I can get this in front of people.” Wachowski added that the script, which she co-wrote with her partner, Mickey Ray Mahoney, “was extremely important for me to write.” She continued, “It was a response to what is happening in the world for trans people, and it gave me a hugely cathartic receptacle to dump all of my anger and rage and frustration into.” Despite her funding obstacles, Wachowski said she’s pivoted to other ways to get this story in front of people “that maybe isn’t a $10 million movie,” such as holding a live table read at Los Angeles’ Dynasty Typewriter theater earlier this month. “I’m just going to go out and I’m going to grab that trans joy with all of my friends. And we’re going to hopefully experience this together.” Wachowski said of The Hunted table read. “It’s not the thing that I had imagined it was going to be, but the end result is the same.” In addition to Wachowski and Mahoney, The Hunted is being produced by Lawrence Mattis and Sarah Marie Flores at Anarchists United and Natasha Lyonne at Ariadne Collective. Wachowski is best known for helming 1999’s The Matrix , 2003’s The Matrix Reloaded and 2003’s The Matrix Revolutions alongside her sister, Lana Wachowski. She’s also directed 1996’s Bound , 2005’s Speed Racer , 2012’s Cloud Atlas and 2015’s Jupiter Ascending , as well as co-created the TV series Sense8 . THR

title: Bob Iger’s New Magic Kingdom: Fans & Media Wonder If He Can Bring That Disney Sparkle To The Lakers
full_text: Skip to main content By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Bob Iger’s New Magic Kingdom: Fans & Media Wonder If He Can Bring That Disney Sparkle To The Lakers Lionsgate Stock Falls To 4-Month Low After Activist Investor Pushes AI Agenda Alex Cooper’s Unwell Media Company Valued At $500M After Investment By Patrick Whitesell’s Firm View All August 12, 2026 6:47pm Bob Iger, former Disney CEO and now one of the principal owners of the Los Angeles Lakers Jordan Teller/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images As the new co-owner of the Los Angeles Lakers , Bob Iger brings with him arguably the most significant Hollywood profile of any owner in the history of U.S. major professional sports. The question fans and Angelenos have now is: What kind of Disney magic can he make? Related Stories Executives Bob Iger Buys L.A. Lakers In Record-Setting, $12.5B Post-Disney Move Sports LeBron James Signs With Philadelphia 76ers As “Last Decision”: “I Am So Excited To Energize A New Fan Base” Iger and Josh Kushner unveiled the stunning deal Wednesday morning, saying they pivoted from pursuing an expansion franchise based in Las Vegas to buying the majority stake held by Mark Walter. The whole Lakers negotiation from start to finish took, according to Iger, just 72 hours. In 2025, Walter ended Buss the family’s 46-year dominion over the team by taking control in a deal valuing the Lakers at around $10 billion. It was a new record in U.S. pro sports. A little more than a year later, Iger and Kushner have bought in at a valuation of $12.5 billion, a new record. More than a few eyebrows have been raised about Walter’s entrance and exit from the Lakers given the fact that the billionaire’s corporate empire is currently the subject of a federal investigation. Bill Simmons, founder of The Ringer, a longtime Lakers hater and the head of talk at Spotify, wrote in an X post that “Conspiracy Bill is overheating” after “the most shocking NBA sale in a long time. The Lakers got flipped!” Watch on Deadline A number of fans were stunned by the timing, noting that Walter had steered the Dodgers to two straight titles and seemed a viable longtime owner after the long reign of the Buss family. The Buss family became NBA royalty by presiding over both the “Showtime” run of titles in the 1970s and ’80s with Magic Johnson and Kareem Abdul-Jabaar, and the 2000s-2010s juggernauts featuring Kobe Bryant and Shaquille O’Neal. The Buss family shepherded the franchise capably for decades, but infighting had led to disarray in the front office. The league had also changed. While the Busses were wealthy by nearly any measure, they weren’t rich like the league’s new wave of owners. When Walter came in, Lakers fans were excited to have their very own billionaire in charge. Fans hoped for some facsimile of what Walter has done across town with the Dodgers. The team over in Chavez Ravine has the second-highest payroll in baseball, has invested heavily in beefing up the front office and has won three MLB championships since Walter became majority owner in 2012. And Walter has been investing in the Lakers. In February, he made his most significant change, bringing over the Dodgers’ longtime executive vice president and chief marketing officer, Lon Rosen, as the Lakers’ president of business operations. The franchise’s G-league (or developmental) team was relocated. There were initiatives to bolster the squad’s assistant general manager ranks and its sports science resources. The team also let a number of longtime staffers go last spring. Now, with Walter gone, it is unclear what the team’s direction will be going forward. “We’re not in Kansas anymore,” said Pete Zayas, co-host of the Laker Film Room podcast, after today’s news was announced. “We don’t have the family that had been running it for 40 years. We’re in some different waters for sure.” “Still Sinking In” In an interview with the California Post , Iger didn’t address speculation about what might have motivated the Walter sale. He said the deal “came together in three days,” a remarkably swift timeline. Former majority owner Jeanie Buss, who had agreed with Walter to remain for five years as the team’s governor, is expected to continue for now in that role, Iger said. “We have enormous respect and appreciation for Jeanie, her father and what they’ve contributed to this franchise,” Iger said. The former Disney mogul said the news is “still sinking in” and his role is “very new.” In terms of future plans, he said, “We’re smart enough to know what we know and what we don’t know. It’s just premature to speculate at all about what we plan to do, because frankly, we haven’t made any plans yet. Again, we go into this with an appreciation of who the Lakers are. And we just want to build value from today on.” Iger came on as a minority investor in Kushner’s Thrive Capital in 2022. Earlier this year, Thrive Capital launched a holding company called Thrive Eternal whose investments, said Kushner, would be in “iconic franchises and cultural institutions rooted in tradition, identity, and shared experience” that would could not be easily replaced by digital innovations, but could enhanced by them. That holding company is, according to The Athletic , the vehicle by which Kushner and Iger intend to buy the Lakers. Iger approaches the team’s new era from a fan’s perspective. He has been known for his passion for the NBA and close relationships with prominent players like Chris Paul. In L.A., he is taking over just after the high-profile departure of LeBron James, who headed to Philadelphia in a free-agent deal earlier this summer. That leaves Luka Doncic and Austin Reeves as the team’s primary stars, with a number of questions about the rest of the roster. The Lakers have won 17 total championships. James helped lead them to the one-of-a-kind Covid bubble title in 2020, but their last non-pandemic crown came in 2010. Apart from 2020, their best recent showing in the playoffs has been a Western Conference Finals appearance in 2023 in which they were swept by the Denver Nuggets. Off the court, the team is still one of the league’s most potent money-makers, but there’s plenty of potential to improve the business. According to a recent ranking compiled by Deadline sister publication Sportico , the team’s 2025 revenue was well behind that of the No. 1 NBA franchise, the Golden State Warriors at $833 million. L.A. was also elbowed out by the New York Knicks, which took in $620 million. Crypto.com Arena, the awkwardly-named venue in downtown L.A. once known as Staples Center, is one area where Iger could put his Disney magic to good use. The arena opened in 1999, at a time when downtown was seeing a massive influx in development spending. Today, DTLA’s mojo has ebbed. The NBA’s L.A. Clippers, longtime former tenants at Staples/Crypto.com, opened their own beyond state-of-the-art venue in Inglewood, CA, the Intuit Dome , in 2024. The result? According to Sportico , “The Clippers took the biggest financial leap in 2024-25 in Year 1 of the Intuit Dome at just over $100 million in sponsor revenue, good for second in the NBA.” Iger made his reputation during his time at Disney in part by acquiring Marvel, Fox, Pixar and Lucasfilm, but also by presiding over a successful expansion of the company’s theme park empire. As even Disney super-fans might wincingly acknowledge, he became a master of extracting revenue from the parks . From opening branded areas like Galaxy’s Edge and Avengers Campus to venturing to China with Shanghai Disney to introducing dynamic pricing, Iger proved adept in overseeing experiential businesses. A number of major sports teams, especially in the NBA, have shown that kind of savvy. Surely, a number of moves by the Warriors, from their Rakuten jersey sponsorship to their “Thrive City” mixed-use area around the San Francisco arena they own, have caught Iger’s eye. Rethinking Local Media Then there’s the local media footprint, a key complement to the national NBA rights deals that took effect in 2025. Last year, the Lakers received a hefty $200 million payment from Charter’s Spectrum SportsNet, the regional sports network whose 20-year deal for team rights runs through the 2031-32 season. While the deal is the league’s richest, Walter, according a report last year in Puck, has “shown openness to taking ownership of Spectrum SportsNet away from Charter.” The upside for the cable company is getting the unattractive financials of the RSN off its books. For the former Lakers owner, the appeal was to be able to potentially rework the team’s media plan to take more of an ownership role, as Major League Baseball’s New York Yankees and others do. Iger, as the former overseer of ESPN and the architect of the latter’s recent swap of 10% of its equity for control of NFL media properties like the NFL network, seems to be pretty ideal casting for an owner looking to reinvent TV and streaming. As the RSN model continues to erode, the NBA is among the leagues overhauling its media plan. It is aiming to launch a hub for local rights by the 2027-28 season. ESPN Chairman Jimmy Pitaro, Iger’s former direct report, said at a CNBC conference in June that there is “a local RSN problem that the entire industry is grappling with right now.” The ESPN app, which relaunched in dramatically expanded form a year ago, has been onboarding non-ESPN sports programming like CW game coverage. As leagues grapple with the RSN issue, Pitaro said, “they should be looking for reach, which we can provide.” When Iger returned to the Disney CEO role in 2023 for his second stint, which ended earlier this year when he passed the baton to Josh D’Amaro, his flair for showmanship, on top of his business acumen, was mentioned by many inside the company. That begs the obvious question of how the experience of attending a Laker game might change in the Iger era. Whether they find a new home or remodel the faded Crypto.com, the team has plenty of ways to improve the experience. That said, Laker games have already been an industry staple, with celebrities like Leonardo DiCaprio, Kim Kardashian and Selena Gomez rubbing elbows courtside with industry heavyweights like Jeffrey Katzenberg. As visions of even loftier, star-packed gatherings take flight, some fans haven’t been able to look past the inherent confusion of having one of the most prominent teams in sports change hands twice in 14 months. “How deep are their pockets?” wondered Laker Film Room co-host Darius Soriano. “They just paid an extraordinary amount of money for this franchise, and putting so much money on the table can be tricky. Are you going to follow through on that investment?” Tom Tapp contributed to this report.
